description: Rule-based scam detection patterns for email and SMS analysis. v1.1 updated from research against r/Scams, CAFC bulletins, news reports of active Canadian scam campaigns, and real sample emails (2024-2026). The analyzer evaluates each rule against a parsed message and accumulates weighted scores. Rules are intentionally narrow and composable — a real scam typically trips 3-5 rules, while a legitimate message trips 0-1.
sources: r/Scams subreddit samples (Geek Squad, CRA, Canada Post)
407 ETR fraud awareness bulletins (1,100+ impersonation domains taken down in 2025)
CBC Go Public e-Transfer fraud reporting
University of Waterloo / Guelph CRA student-targeting samples

scoring.notes: Total score is capped at 100. Below 'low', no warning. Between low-medium, subtle indicator. Between medium-high, persistent warning banner. Above 'high', full-page block with override required. Tune in user-facing 'Strict / Balanced / Permissive' setting by shifting thresholds ±15.

rule_types.display_name_domain_mismatch: The display name in From claims an org but the address domain isn't in that org's known_sender_domains (cross-reference known-sender-domains.json).
rule_types.free_provider_claiming_institution: Address is on a free email provider (gmail, outlook, yahoo, proton, hotmail, etc.) but display name or body claims to represent a bank, government agency, or major institution.
rule_types.domain_lookalike: Sender domain is a typo/homoglyph/Levenshtein variant of a known institution domain.
rule_types.suspicious_tld: Sender domain uses a high-abuse TLD (.xyz, .top, .click, .live, .vip, etc.) while claiming institutional identity.
rule_types.suspicious_subdomain_chain: Sender domain has many subdomains used to hide the real registrable domain (e.g., 'cra.gc.ca.refund.xyz').
rule_types.punycode_domain: Sender domain uses punycode (xn--) — almost never legitimate for institutional mail.
rule_types.reply_to_mismatch: Reply-To domain differs from From domain in a way that suggests a forward-mail trick.
rule_types.urgency_language: Body contains urgency triggers: 'within 24 hours', 'immediate action required', 'account will be suspended', 'final notice', 'warrant', 'arrest'.
rule_types.payment_red_flag: Body requests payment via gift cards (iTunes, Google Play, Amazon, Steam), cryptocurrency, Interac e-Transfer to an individual, wire transfer, or prepaid cards.
rule_types.credential_request: Body asks for SIN, full credit card number, banking login, CVV, online banking password, or one-time code.
rule_types.callback_number_in_invoice: Body presents a high-dollar charge and instructs the reader to call a phone number to dispute. Hallmark of Geek Squad/Norton/McAfee scams.
rule_types.link_text_url_mismatch: Visible link text shows one domain but href points elsewhere (e.g., 'rbc.com' linking to 'rbc-secure-login.com').
rule_types.shortened_link_to_institution: Body uses a URL shortener (bit.ly, tinyurl, t.co, goo.gl) for what claims to be an institutional link.
rule_types.ip_address_link: A link points to a raw IP address rather than a domain.
rule_types.attachment_with_executable: Message has an attachment with executable or scripting extension (.exe, .scr, .vbs, .js, .iso, .lnk, password-protected .zip).
rule_types.html_form_in_email: Email body contains an HTML <form> element requesting credentials — legitimate orgs link to their site, they don't embed forms.
rule_types.sin_request: Body explicitly asks for Social Insurance Number — no legitimate Canadian institution requests SIN via email.
rule_types.etransfer_to_individual: Body instructs sending Interac e-Transfer to a personal-looking email address rather than to a recipient identifiable as the org.
rule_types.auth_header_failure: Parsed authentication-results header shows SPF, DKIM, or DMARC failure for a claimed institutional sender. Strongest single signal when present.
rule_types.language_mix_anomaly: Mixing of English/French in a way characteristic of automated translation — common in scams targeting bilingual Canada from non-Canadian operators. Defined for future use; no rule currently references it.
rule_types.recent_registration: Sender domain registered within the last 90 days. Defined for future use; no rule currently references it because it requires WHOIS lookup integration.
rule_types.imessage_evasion_pattern: Body contains the 'reply Y, then exit and re-open the message to activate the link' trick. Apple disables links in iMessage from unknown senders; this pattern exists solely to defeat that protection and is a near-certain scam signal.
rule_types.toll_road_smishing: SMS or email claims unpaid toll, threatens license/registration suspension, links to non-official domain. Top-volume Canadian scam category as of 2025-2026.
rule_types.license_revocation_threat: Message threatens revocation/suspension of driver's licence, vehicle registration, or denial of plate renewal by ServiceOntario or equivalent. Used in toll, parking, and traffic-ticket scams.
rule_types.sin_disclosure_in_message: The message ITSELF contains the recipient's SIN (typically the last 3 digits or full SIN) used as a manufactured proof of legitimacy. CAFC reported this pattern in 2024 — confirms the sender has access to leaked data, but legitimate CRA messages do not include SIN in transactional text.
rule_types.ai_generated_indicators: Generic AI tells: perfect grammar despite institutional impersonation, em-dashes used in transactional text, 'I hope this message finds you well' openings, unusually polished language combined with other red flags. NOT diagnostic on its own — only used as a tiebreaker.
rule_types.etransfer_loading_screen_phish: Page or message references an e-Transfer 'loading' screen or 'processing... do not refresh' messaging combined with a request to log into a bank. Pattern from active 2025 Canadian e-Transfer interception scams.
rule_types.package_redelivery_fee: Message claims a package can't be delivered without paying a small fee ($1-$5 typical) via a link. Canada Post / Purolator / FedEx variant — Canada Post explicitly does not use this pattern.
rule_types.auto_renewal_callback_combo: Combined fingerprint: 'auto-renewed' or 'subscription' or 'order settled' + a callback phone number + dollar amount. Almost 100% diagnostic of the Best Buy/Geek Squad/Norton invoice scam.
rule_types.fake_2fa_security_alert: Message claims 'unusual sign-in', 'verify your account', 'someone logged in from [location]' with a link to 'secure your account'. Modern account-takeover phishing template.
rule_types.alberta_affordability_scam: Claims to be from Government of Alberta offering an affordability/energy rebate registration via link. Confirmed scam pattern flagged by the Alberta government.
rule_types.concession_a25_scam: Claims to be Concession A25 toll bridge (Laval-Montréal) with payment link. Real A25 communications go through a25.com.

rules.description: Address is gmail/outlook/yahoo/etc. but display name or body references CRA, Revenue Canada, or ARC.
rules.user_explanation: The Canada Revenue Agency does not send email from Gmail, Outlook, or any free email provider.

rules.description: Free-provider sender claiming Service Canada.
rules.user_explanation: Service Canada does not use free email services.

rules.description: Free-provider sender claiming IRCC / Immigration Canada — common newcomer scam.
rules.user_explanation: IRCC communicates through your online account at canada.ca, not from free email addresses. Newcomers are heavily targeted by this scam.

rules.description: Free-provider sender claiming a Canadian bank.
rules.user_explanation: Canadian banks never send account communications from free email providers like Gmail or Outlook.

rules.description: Free-provider sender claiming Interac e-Transfer.
rules.user_explanation: Interac e-Transfer notifications come from notify.payments.interac.ca, never from Gmail or other free providers.

rules.description: Free-provider sender claiming RCMP or police force — almost always sextortion or fake-warrant scam.
rules.user_explanation: Canadian police forces do not contact people via Gmail or other free email providers. Any 'warrant' or 'investigation' email is a scam.

rules.description: Domain claims CRA but uses a high-abuse TLD instead of .gc.ca or .canada.ca.
rules.user_explanation: Canada Revenue Agency emails always come from .gc.ca or .canada.ca — never from .xyz, .top, .click, or similar TLDs.

rules.description: Display claims Canadian government but domain isn't .gc.ca or .canada.ca.
rules.user_explanation: Federal Government of Canada emails come from .gc.ca or .canada.ca domains. Any other domain claiming to be the federal government is suspicious.

rules.description: Sender domain is within Levenshtein distance 2 of a high_value entry in the institution whitelist, or differs only by homoglyph substitution.
rules.user_explanation: The sender domain looks similar to a real institution but isn't an exact match. Scammers register near-duplicate domains to fool quick readers.

rules.description: Sender domain uses punycode (xn--) and the message claims institutional identity.
rules.user_explanation: The sender uses an internationalized domain name that displays as recognizable letters but encodes to different characters underneath. No major Canadian institution uses punycode email domains.

rules.description: From domain contains an institution name as a subdomain but the registrable domain is something else (e.g., 'cra.gc.ca.refund-portal.xyz').
rules.user_explanation: The institution name appears in the subdomain to trick the reader, but the actual domain is something else. The part right before .com / .ca is what matters.

rules.description: Message instructs sending Interac e-Transfer to a personal-looking email rather than to an institutional recipient.
rules.user_explanation: Real institutions don't receive payment via e-Transfer to a personal Gmail or Yahoo address. This is a hallmark of refund and rental scams.

rules.description: Body requests payment via gift cards.
rules.user_explanation: No legitimate institution, government agency, or business ever accepts payment via gift cards. Any request for gift-card payment is a scam — full stop.

rules.description: Body requests payment in cryptocurrency.
rules.user_explanation: No Canadian government agency, bank, or utility accepts cryptocurrency as payment. Requests for crypto are a scam signal regardless of context.

rules.description: Body requests Social Insurance Number.
rules.user_explanation: No legitimate organization will request your Social Insurance Number via email. SIN should only be given over established phone lines or in person to verified institutions.

rules.description: Body uses arrest/warrant urgency language.
rules.user_explanation: Canadian law enforcement does not warn people of impending arrest by email or SMS. This language is designed to create panic.

rules.description: Body uses 24-hour deadline language.
rules.user_explanation: Artificial deadlines are a manipulation tactic. Legitimate institutions give reasonable notice and allow you to verify by calling them directly.

rules.description: Body requests password or login credentials directly.
rules.user_explanation: No legitimate institution will ever ask for your password by email. Real password resets always happen via a link to the institution's own site.

rules.description: Body requests a one-time code or 2FA code.

body_contains_any: reply with the code we just texted

rules.user_explanation: One-time codes are a second authentication factor — sharing them by reply defeats their purpose. This is a hallmark of account-takeover scams.

rules.description: Message uses a URL shortener for what claims to be an institutional link.
rules.user_explanation: Canadian banks, the CRA, and major institutions do not use URL shorteners — they use full, recognizable links to their own domains.

rules.description: Visible link text shows an institutional domain but href points to a different domain.
rules.user_explanation: The link displays one address but actually leads somewhere else. This is one of the most reliable scam signals.

rules.description: Message contains a link to a raw IP address.
rules.user_explanation: Real institutional emails never link directly to an IP address. This pattern is used to evade domain reputation checks.

rules.description: Email contains an HTML form requesting input.
rules.user_explanation: Legitimate institutions never embed login or payment forms inside emails. They always link out to their own website.

rules.description: Message has an executable, script, or password-protected archive attachment.
rules.user_explanation: Canadian institutions never send executable files or password-protected archives by email. Any such attachment is almost certainly malware.

rules.description: From appears institutional but Reply-To points to a free-email provider.
rules.user_explanation: The visible From appears to be an institution, but replies would go to a personal Gmail or Outlook address. This is a near-certain spoofing signal.

rules.description: Authentication-Results header shows SPF/DKIM/DMARC failure for a sender claiming a known brand.
rules.user_explanation: The email's authentication checks failed for the institution it claims to be from. This means the sender almost certainly forged the From address.

rules.description: Body contains the 'reply Y then exit and re-open the message' trick to bypass iMessage link-blocking for unknown senders. Source: real samples from 407 ETR toll, FastTrak, and other 2025 smishing campaigns.

body_contains_any: exit the text message and open it again
copy the link into your Safari
open it in your Safari browser

rules.user_explanation: This is a known trick to bypass iMessage's protection that blocks links from unknown senders. Apple does this on purpose — if a message is telling you to 'reply Y and reopen', it is almost certainly a scam.

rules.description: Classic unpaid-toll smishing template. 407 ETR alone took down 1,100+ impersonation domains in 2025. Mirrors FastTrak (US) and EZDriveMA scam structures.
rules.user_explanation: Real 407 ETR text messages do NOT contain a direct payment link. To check whether you actually owe a toll, log in at 407etr.com directly, never through a link in a message.

rules.description: Message threatens driver's licence revocation, vehicle registration suspension, or plate renewal denial. Used in toll, parking-ticket, and Service Ontario scams.
rules.user_explanation: Threats of immediate licence or registration revocation by text or email are a scam tactic. Real licence-related actions in Canada are handled by mail through the provincial transport ministry, not by surprise SMS.

rules.description: Message contains what appears to be the recipient's SIN as proof of legitimacy. CAFC flagged this pattern in early 2024 — scammers obtained SINs from prior breaches and use them to seem credible. CRA does NOT include SIN in transactional message body.
rules.user_explanation: A scam may show your real SIN to seem legitimate — this means your data was leaked previously, NOT that the sender is real. Canadian government agencies do not include full or partial SINs in unsolicited messages.

rules.description: Tight fingerprint based on real 2025 Geek Squad scam samples. Subject 'Payment order settled' / 'Subscription renewed', greeting 'Dear User' or 'Dear Customer', dollar amount $200-$700, callback number with toll-free prefix.
rules.user_explanation: This message matches the exact template of the most-reported Canadian invoice scam (Geek Squad / Norton / McAfee). The phone number does not lead to Best Buy — it leads to a fraudster who will ask for remote computer access or gift-card payment. Real Best Buy charges appear on your credit card statement; check there first, never call a number from the email.

rules.description: References to an e-Transfer 'loading' or 'processing' screen with instructions not to refresh. Pattern from 2024 Fredericton case and similar Kijiji/Marketplace e-Transfer interception scams.

body_contains_any: this may take a few minutes

rules.user_explanation: Real Interac e-Transfer deposits complete in seconds through your bank's own login. A 'loading' or 'processing' screen on a non-bank page is a phishing tool designed to capture your banking login while pretending to process the deposit.

rules.description: Canada Post / Purolator / FedEx 'small redelivery fee' template. Active for years and remains a top SMS-reported scam in Canada.
rules.user_explanation: Real Canada Post never asks for a small redelivery fee via SMS or email link. Real undelivered packages can be retrieved at your local post office. To verify, search the tracking number at canadapost.ca directly.

rules.description: Generic 'unusual sign-in' / 'verify your account' template with a link. Most commonly impersonates Microsoft, Apple, Netflix, banks, or Amazon.

body_contains_any: someone tried to log into your account
click here to confirm it was you
if this wasn't you, click here
your account has been temporarily limited

rules.user_explanation: Account security alerts should always be verified by logging into the service directly through its app or by typing the address yourself — never by clicking a link in the message.

rules.description: Government of Alberta 'affordability payment' or 'energy rebate' SMS scam. Confirmed by the Alberta government 2022-2025.
rules.user_explanation: Government of Alberta does not send rebate or affordability-payment registration links by text. Real benefits arrive via your existing CRA direct deposit setup.

rules.description: Concession A25 toll bridge (Laval-Montréal) impersonation. CAFC-confirmed pattern 2024+.
rules.user_explanation: Real A25 toll communications direct you to a25.com directly. Texts with payment links claiming unpaid bridge tolls are a confirmed scam pattern in Quebec.

rules.description: Specific CRA-tax-refund-via-e-Transfer template. Verbatim phrases pulled from 2020 Waterloo student scam wave and still circulating.
rules.user_explanation: CRA does NOT use Interac e-Transfer to send refunds. Refunds come by direct deposit (if set up) or by cheque, never via an Interac e-Transfer link. This message template is verbatim from documented scam campaigns.

rules.description: Late-stage scam pivot to gift cards after initial contact (commonly seen in CRA phone-pivot-to-email and tech-support remote-access scams).

body_contains_any: go to the nearest store and purchase
scratch off the back and send
send us the codes on the back

rules.user_explanation: No legitimate organization accepts gift cards as payment. If a 'CRA agent', 'Microsoft tech', 'police officer', or any other authority asks you to buy gift cards from a store and read the codes back, hang up — full stop.

rules.description: Tiebreaker rule: polished, AI-generated-sounding language combined with at least one other red flag. AI scams are now 82.6% of phishing (per industry reporting), so grammar is no longer a useful exclusion criterion.
rules.user_explanation: Modern scams use AI to write perfectly. Good grammar is no longer evidence that an email is genuine.
